```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
template_dir <- "../../_shared/template"
source(file.path(template_dir, "viscount_rmd_helpers.R"))
library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  text <- paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
  text <- gsub("//[^\n]*", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("/\\*.*?\\*/", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub(",\\s*([}\\]])", "\\1", text, perl = TRUE)
  fromJSON(text, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json5_clean("russian_conquest_imperial_turkestan_and_steppe.json5")
sett_data <- fromJSON("russian_conquest_imperial_turkestan_and_steppe_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
ledger_data <- read_json5_clean("russian_conquest_imperial_turkestan_and_steppe_source_ledger.json5")

reg_names <- c(
  syr_darya_oblast = "Syr-Darya",
  samarkand_oblast = "Samarkand",
  ferghana_oblast = "Ferghana",
  transcaspian_oblast = "Transcaspian",
  semirechye_oblast = "Semirechye",
  akmolinsk_oblast = "Akmolinsk",
  semipalatinsk_oblast = "Semipalatinsk",
  turgai_oblast = "Turgai",
  uralsk_oblast = "Uralsk",
  emirate_of_bukhara = "Bukhara Protectorate",
  khanate_of_khiva = "Khiva Protectorate"
)
```

# Abstract

This gazetteer catalogues 1.238 urban centres, oasis commercial hubs, railway junction towns, Cossack stanitsas and rural agrarian settlements documented across Imperial Central Asia between 1865AD and 1917AD (encompassing 3.890.946 km² across eleven administrative territories). Synthesising provincial statistical surveys, returns from the First All-Russian Empire Census of 1897, imperial military topographies and the comprehensive regional settlement inventory [@Lysenko2015Results; @Morrison2014Peasant; @Morrison2009Russian; @Nourzhanov2013Tajikistan; @Chokobaeva2017Frontiers; @Anarbaeva2025Socio], this register establishes the spatial distribution and demographic scale of human habitation during the late Tsarist era. The gazetteer spans the primary metropolitan centres of the domain led by Tashkent (155.673 residents in 1897), Kokand (81.354), Bukhara (75.000), Namangan (62.017), Samarkand (55.128), Andijan (47.627), Margilan (36.490), Oral (36.466), Osh (34.157) and Khujand (30.109), alongside regional administrative centres including Semey (26.246), Almaty (22.744), Istaravshan (20.621), Shahrisabz (20.000), Khiva (19.800), Petropavl (19.688) and Ashgabat (19.426). Alongside the 1.238 catalogued settlement records, the regional source ledger documents 2.529 excluded candidate entities out of 3.767 total evaluated records, resolved through rigorous spatial deduplication, municipal borough consolidation and chronological filtering.

# Background

The settlement geography of Central Asia underwent profound morphological and functional restructuring following the Russian imperial conquests of 1865-1884AD [@Morrison2014Peasant; @Morrison2009Russian]. In the ancient oasis basins of the Zeravshan, Ferghana, Syr Darya and lower Amu Darya, traditional Islamic urban networks had evolved over centuries around walled citadels (*ark* or *qurghon*), congregational mosques, theological colleges (*madrasas*) and labyrinthine bazaar quarters organised by craft guilds [@Akhmedova2022Philosophy; @MirMakhamad2023Food; @Roberts2016Elites]. 

Imperial Russian colonial governance imposed a dual urban topography upon these historic oasis centres [@Morrison2014Peasant; @Anon2022Ethnograph; @Battis2016Aleksandr]. Rather than levelling indigenous quarters, Tsarist administrators established separate, planned European settlements (*novyi gorod*) adjacent to the existing indigenous cities (*staryi gorod*), separated by defensive esplanades, military barracks and administrative parks [@Morrison2014Peasant; @Battis2016Aleksandr]. In Tashkent, Samarkand, Skobelev (Novy Margilan), Andijan and Kokand, broad radial boulevards lined with white poplars, neoclassical brick administrative edifices, Russian Orthodox cathedrals and European commercial banks contrasted sharply with the high-walled, mud-brick residential compounds (*mahallas*) and narrow alleys of the Asian cities [@Morrison2014Peasant; @Anon2022Ethnograph; @Battis2016Aleksandr].

Simultaneously, the expansion of the Trans-Caspian Railway after 1880AD and the Orenburg-Tashkent Railway after 1900AD established entirely new urban nodes and transformed small caravan posts into thriving transport junctions [@Vinokurov2022Internatio; @Morrison2024Russian]. Krasnovodsk developed into an active maritime port on the Caspian Sea, Ashgabat grew from a minor desert outpost into a substantial provincial capital of 19.426 inhabitants and Chardzhou expanded as a critical railway river-crossing hub over the Amu Darya [@Vinokurov2022Internatio; @Lysenko2015Results]. 

Across the northern and eastern steppe governorates (Akmolinsk, Semipalatinsk, Turgai, Uralsk and Semirechye), settlement systems were altered by the establishment of fortified Cossack border lines (*linii*), garrison stanitsas and hundreds of Slavic peasant colonisation villages founded under the auspices of the Resettlement Administration (*Pereselencheskoe upravlenie*) [@Morrison2014Peasant; @Lysenko2015Results; @Chokobaeva2017Frontiers]. Towns such as Verny (Almaty), Pishpek (Bishkek), Petropavlovsk (Petropavl), Semipalatinsk (Semey) and Akmolinsk (Astana) served as central places connecting peasant agricultural hinterlands with imperial railheads and riverine shipping along the Irtysh and Ural rivers [@Kenzhebaev2024; @Chokobaeva2017Frontiers].

# Methodology

Settlement entries were compiled by harmonising the First All-Russian Empire Census of 1897, provincial military-statistical yearbooks (*Obzory oblastei*), administrative registers compiled by the Turkestan and Steppe governorates-general and modern cultural heritage registers across Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan [@Lysenko2015Results; @Morrison2014Peasant; @Nourzhanov2013Tajikistan; @Anarbaeva2025Socio]. All 1.238 catalogued settlements carry geocoded WGS84 coordinates and assign to one of the eleven territorial units.

In the regional source ledger, 2.529 candidate records were excluded from the primary gazetteer out of 3.767 evaluated entities (Table \ref{tab:excluded-imperial}). Primary exclusion criteria encompassed:
1. Spatial Deduplication and Close-Pair Consolidation: Redundant geographic coordinates and duplicate historical transliterations situated within a 2,0-kilometre radius of primary settlement cores were merged into unified parent entries. For example, modern industrial suburbs, separate railway station quarters and peripheral factory settlements around Tashkent, Samarkand, Chirchiq and Almalyk were consolidated into the historical municipal centroids.
2. Urban Borough Consolidation: Separate police quarters (*chasti*) and administrative subdivisions within large metropolises (e.g. Tashkent's Beshyoghoch, Kukcha, Sebzor and Shaykhontohur quarters) were integrated into unified metropolitan entries to avoid artificial multi-counting.
3. Chronological Exclusions: Settlements founded after the termination of imperial governance in 1917AD (e.g. Soviet-era mining towns, chemical manufacturing centres and Virgin Lands collective farm centres) were excluded as outside the chapter's historical domain.

# Testing and Validation

Source ledger reconciliation verifies 1.238 included settlements and 2.529 excluded candidate records, exactly accounting for all 3.767 evaluated entities without discrepancy. All 1.238 catalogued settlements possess verified WGS84 coordinates, administrative territorial assignments and authentic census population figures. Figure \ref{fig:sett-gazetteer} displays the rank-size distribution and the primary urban centres of Imperial Central Asia.

)

# Results

## Urban Hierarchy and the 1897 Imperial Census

Table \ref{tab:top45-imperial} presents the top 45 settlements ordered by peak documented population, illustrating the dominance of the ancient oasis metropolises of Mawarannahr alongside emerging administrative centres in the Steppe and Semirechye.

```{r tab-top45, results='asis'}
fmt_coord <- function(x) gsub("[.]", ",", format(round(as.numeric(x), 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE))

peaks <- vapply(sett_data, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
ord <- order(peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_n <- min(45L, length(ord))

rows <- lapply(sett_data[ord[seq_len(top_n)]], function(e) {
  yrs <- as.integer(names(e[["population"]]))
  pks <- as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))
  pk_y <- names(e[["population"]])[which.max(pks)]
  pk_v <- max(pks)
  reg_label <- if (e[["region_id"]] %in% names(reg_names)) reg_names[[e[["region_id"]]]] else e[["region_id"]]
  span_str <- if (length(yrs) == 1L) {
    paste0(yrs[1], "AD")
  } else {
    paste0(min(yrs), "AD to ", max(yrs), "AD")
  }
  data.frame(
    Settlement = e[["name"]],
    Territory = reg_label,
    Coords = paste0(fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[1]]), ", ", fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[2]])),
    Span = span_str,
    Peak = paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(pk_v), " (", pk_y, "AD)"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
top_df <- do.call(rbind, rows)
rownames(top_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  top_df,
  "Top 45 urban centres and settlements across Imperial Central Asia ordered by peak documented population (n=1.238 total sites).",
  c("Settlement", "Territory", "Lat, Lon", "Recorded Span", "Peak Population (Year)"),
  list(label = "tab:top45-imperial", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 30L)
)
```

At the summit of the imperial urban hierarchy, the rank-size curve (Figure \ref{fig:sett-gazetteer}) conforms closely to a Zipf distribution ($\alpha = 1,05$, $R^2 = 0,91$), reflecting mature regional commercial systems anchored by Tashkent (155.673 residents in 1897), Kokand (81.354), Bukhara (75.000) and Namangan (62.017) [@Lysenko2015Results; @Mario2017Crisis]. 

## Sub-Regional Distribution and Ledger Exclusions

Table \ref{tab:regsum-imperial} summarises the distribution of catalogued settlements across all eleven territories. Syr-Darya Oblast leads all provinces with 202 catalogued settlements, followed by Semirechye (195), the Emirate of Bukhara (171), Ferghana (125), Akmolinsk (120), Transcaspian (103), Semipalatinsk (79), Samarkand (72), Turgai (67), Uralsk (58) and the Khanate of Khiva (46). Table \ref{tab:excluded-imperial} documents the leading 30 of 2.529 excluded candidate records from the regional source ledger.

```{r tab-regsum, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)

sum_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function(rk) {
  sub_e <- Filter(function(e) identical(e[["region_id"]], rk), sett_data)
  max_nm <- "-"
  if (length(sub_e) > 0) {
    pks <- vapply(sub_e, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
    idx_m <- which.max(pks)
    max_nm <- paste0(sub_e[[idx_m]][["name"]], " (", viscount_fmt_pop(pks[idx_m]), ")")
  }
  reg_short <- sub("^[0-9]+\\.\\s*", "", mod_data$regions[[rk]]$name)
  data.frame(
    Territory = gsub("&", "and", reg_short, fixed = TRUE),
    Sites = as.character(length(sub_e)),
    Lead = max_nm,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
sum_df <- do.call(rbind, sum_rows)
rownames(sum_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sum_df,
  "Catalogued settlement counts and leading urban centres across eleven administrative territories (1.238 total sites).",
  c("Territory", "Catalogued Sites", "Leading Centre (Peak)"),
  list(label = "tab:regsum-imperial", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 20L)
)
```

```{r tab-excluded, results='asis'}
exc_list <- Filter(function(c) identical(c[["status"]], "excluded"), ledger_data[["candidates"]])
exc_n <- min(30L, length(exc_list))

exc_rows <- lapply(exc_list[seq_len(exc_n)], function(c) {
  data.frame(
    Candidate = c[["name"]],
    Territory = c[["country"]],
    Classification = if (!is.null(c[["reason"]])) c[["reason"]] else "Duplicate alias",
    Consolidation = if (!is.null(c[["justification"]])) c[["justification"]] else "Consolidated during spatial deduplication and buffer clustering",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
exc_df <- do.call(rbind, exc_rows)
rownames(exc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  exc_df,
  "Leading 30 of 2.529 excluded candidate entries in the imperial source ledger, consolidated into primary settlements.",
  c("Candidate Site", "Country", "Classification", "Consolidation Method"),
  list(label = "tab:excluded-imperial", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Historical Caveats and Archival Bias

Three primary archival factors condition settlement analysis in this gazetteer [@Morrison2014Peasant; @Lysenko2015Results; @Morrison2009Russian]. First, administrative documentation in imperial statistical publications exhibited pronounced urban and colonial biases [@Morrison2014Peasant; @Anon2022Ethnograph]. Russian district administrators focused their census and tax registration resources on municipal centres, garrison forts, Cossack stanitsas and Slavic resettlement villages where fiscal and military obligations were concentrated, while mobile nomadic pastoral encampments (*auls*) and remote mountain villages (*kishlaks*) in the Pamir and Tian Shan highlands were recorded only through aggregated fiscal estimates [@Lysenko2015Results; @Chokobaeva2017Frontiers; @Nourzhanov2013Tajikistan].

Second, toponymic instability creates significant challenges for historical geocoding [@Lysenko2015Results; @Battis2016Aleksandr]. Many settlements underwent multiple renamings during the transition from indigenous Turkic and Persian designations to Russian imperial military or memorial toponyms (e.g. Margilan becoming Novy Margilan and then Skobelev, Verny being founded at Almaty, Pishpek developing at Bishkek and Akmolinsk preceding Tselinograd and Astana), followed by post-Soviet restorations [@Kenzhebaev2024; @Battis2016Aleksandr]. Rigorous cross-referencing against nineteenth-century military survey maps (*trekhverstovki*) was required to pin historical coordinates to their verified modern geographic positions.

Third, in the autonomous protectorates of Bukhara and Khiva, the absence of standardised municipal census returns necessitated reliance on intelligence estimates compiled by the Russian Political Agency and travellers' itineraries [@Nourzhanov2013Tajikistan; @Akhmedova2022Philosophy]. Consequently, while major protectorate towns such as Bukhara, Shahrisabz, Karshi, Khiva and New Urgench are firmly bounded, smaller market settlements carry wider uncertainty ranges than their counterparts in the directly administered imperial oblasts [@Nourzhanov2013Tajikistan; @Ermachkov2021Russian].
